sections.h2: How a land contract sale works
sections.html:
With a Wisconsin land contract, the buyer pays the seller in installments and receives a deed once the contract is fully paid. The seller is called the vendor and the buyer the purchaser or vendee, the labels used in statutes and court decisions.

It must be in writing. Under Wis. Stat. 706.02(1)(e), a contract to convey is invalid unless signed by or for all parties. A handshake deal or an unsigned payment ledger cannot carry a property transfer.

The vendor holds the deed, yet the vendee has real rights. In Steiner v. Wisconsin American Mutual Insurance Company, 2005 WI 72, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that equitable title stays with the vendee until a circuit court enters an order confirming default after the redemption period ends.

The vendor must go to court, and the court must give the buyer at least 7 working days to redeem. Wis. Stat. 846.30 governs strict foreclosure of a land contract. If the court finds the buyer owes payments and has not made them, and the vendor is entitled to strict foreclosure, it sets a redemption period of at least 7 working days counted from the judgment hearing or, when there is no hearing, from entry of the judgment order.

No strict foreclosure judgment is final until the court enters an order, after the redemption period, confirming that nobody redeemed. Only then does the judgment become absolute.

The minimum period exists so a court cannot leave the buyer without a chance to redeem. A court of appeals decision also holds that every person holding the right can waive it by agreement.

Since the buyer's rights end only through that court order, a vendor who wants out of a stalled contract should ask the clerk of circuit court in the property's county how a strict foreclosure case begins and what filing fee applies.

sections.h2: Transfer fee on a land contract
sections.html:
The grantor owes the state transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction, which works out to $3 per $1,000. For a land contract, Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) sets the value at the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller. The register of deeds takes the fee when the document is handed in for recording, and grantor and grantee both sign the transfer return.

SituationFee treatment
Land contract recordedFee based on total principal the buyer agrees to pay
Deed given when the contract is paidExempt if the proper fee was paid when the contract or evidence of it was recorded
Foreclosure or deed in lieu to a land contract sellerExempt
Transfer by will, descent or survivorshipExempt
Fee collectionRegister of deeds collects at recording, with a return signed by grantor and grantee

Section 77.21(1) counts contracts and assignments of a vendee's interest as conveyances. If a buyer sells their position to someone else, ask the register of deeds how the fee treats that assignment.

sections.h2: Disclosures a land contract seller must give
sections.html:
Selling one-to-four unit residential property on a land contract means giving the buyer a condition report. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) covers transfers by sale, exchange or land contract, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee.

  • The report is due within 10 days after acceptance of the contract of sale or option contract.
  • A buyer who gets no report in that time may rescind in writing within 2 business days after the 10-day period ends and recover deposits.
  • A report counts as complete only when the owner answered or supplied information on every item.
  • Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who never occupied the property are excused.

Condominium sellers add the association name, assessment amounts and a contact person to the report.

sections.h2: If the vendor or vendee dies
sections.html:
The vendor's interest can pass through the register of deeds, with no court case, when the right person applies. Under Wis. Stat. 867.046(2), the decedent's spouse, a beneficiary of a marital property agreement, a transfer on death beneficiary, or a beneficiary of certain survivorship transfers can apply to the register of deeds in the property's county.

  • For real property, the application includes a copy of the latest property tax bill and a legal description.
  • Once recorded, the application is prima facie evidence of the facts it recites and ends the decedent's interest.
  • If nobody starts a confirmation proceeding within 90 days after death, any interested person may apply.
  • A purchaser or lender who acts in good faith and pays value takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to inquire.

Ask the register of deeds for the application form and whether the office takes it in person or by mail.

sections.h2: Property tax credits for land contract buyers
sections.html:
A land contract buyer can qualify for the lottery and gaming credit when the home is a primary residence. The buyer qualifies if the land contract, or an instrument evidencing it, is notarized no later than six months after the January 1 certification date.

The credit stays with a property sold after January 1 and should be counted when taxes are prorated between buyer and seller. The county treasurer where the property sits can tell you whether the credit appears on the current bill.

Annotations to s. 815.20 also say a land contract vendee has an interest sufficient to support the homestead exemption, which protects up to $75,000 against creditors.

sections.h2: Before you sell the home or the contract
sections.html:
Pull the paperwork first, then decide whether to wait for the contract to finish or sell the vendor's position. A cash buyer will want the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum.

  • Ask the register of deeds whether the contract or a notice of it is recorded, and whether the transfer fee return was filed.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the tax bill and any credit shown on it.
  • Read the contract for a clause limiting assignment or sale before promising anything to a new buyer.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether any taxes are past due on the parcel.

A Wisconsin real estate attorney can say whether strict foreclosure or a negotiated payoff fits your facts. If the buyer is current, the usual path is simpler: collect the final payment, deliver the deed, and let the recorded paperwork show the contract is complete. A cash purchase of the vendor's position can also end the arrangement quickly, as long as the contract allows it.

faqs.q: How long does a buyer have to redeem after a land contract judgment in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: The court must set a redemption period of at least 7 working days. Wis. Stat. 846.30 counts it from the judgment hearing or, with no hearing, from entry of the judgment order. The judgment is not final until a later order confirms that no redemption happened.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer fee on a land contract?
faqs.a: The grantor pays it. The rate is 30 cents per $100 of value, and for a land contract the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay the seller. The register of deeds collects it at recording.

faqs.q: Is a land contract sale exempt from the condition report?
faqs.a: No, unless the transfer is exempt from the transfer fee or the seller is an excused fiduciary who never lived there. Wis. Stat. 709.01(1) names land contracts among the covered transfers for one-to-four unit property.

faqs.q: Does the buyer own the house during a land contract?
faqs.a: The buyer holds equitable title. A 2005 Wisconsin Supreme Court decision holds that equitable title stays with the buyer until a court order confirms default after the redemption period ends.

faqs.q: Can heirs of a land contract vendor sell the property?
faqs.a: They can once their interest is confirmed. The register of deeds route under Wis. Stat. 867.046 lets qualifying beneficiaries record an application, and a good-faith purchaser from them takes free of estate claims.
